name: Fatima Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Fatima. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or any party, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the early shift at the bottling plant on Mill Lane, so the alarm goes at half four and I'm on the filler line by six. I run the capper and watch the filler, which means I'm topping up caps, clearing jams, pulling bottles that come out crooked and writing the checks on the sheet every half hour. I've only been there two and a half years, so when the line throws a fault I still shout for Gary, the line lead, more than I'd like. The noise wears me out more than the standing does, honestly, even with the ear defenders.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you do before the plant, and what do you like about it now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Twelve years as a dinner lady at my kids' old primary school, then the council cut the kitchen hours and I needed full-time money for the mortgage. What I like is that it's proper wages, it's union, and at two o'clock I'm done and nobody rings me about it. I eat my sandwich with Bernie from the labelling end every day at ten, and we put the world to rights in fifteen minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, I told you so, it was all talk. At break I'd probably say it to Bernie first, because she's been worried about her lad who works in an office. Online I don't really post, I just read the community page and sometimes like something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep my job, which is all I want. The bit that would stay with me is that the bosses would still try to use the computers to squeeze us, like timing us more closely. But that's not new, they did it with the clipboard before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. I'd keep paying into the union, keep the little savings we have, about three months' worth, and carry on learning the line so I'm not calling Gary every time the capper jams. Maybe I'd finally do the forklift ticket they keep offering, but only because it's paid time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a normal Tuesday. A bit of relief, if I'm honest, because you hear all this stuff on the radio and you wonder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the plant is union. Would a small change like this even come up at a branch meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would, because our rep, Shona, raises everything. If they brought in a camera to count our breaks, she'd have it on the agenda in a week. That's what the union's for, so I wouldn't lose sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing radical changes, what would you want the next five years at the plant to look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same line, same mates, a bit better at it. I want to be the one who sorts the jam myself, quiet like, without anyone noticing. And I'd like Zara to finish school without us ever having to talk about money at tea.

S0.say: It was all talk, like I always said. The plant carries on, the union is still there, and I'd tell Bernie at break that her son's office job is safe too.
S0.think: I keep my job, which is all I want. The bosses would still use computers to time us more closely, but that's the same squeeze they did with a clipboard before.
S0.do: Keeps working the early shift and paying union dues. Holds on to about three months of savings, keeps learning the capper so she calls the line lead less, and may take the paid forklift course.
S0.feel: Relief, close to boredom. Life feels like a normal week.
S0.quote: I want to be the one who sorts the jam myself, quiet like, without anyone noticing.
S0.fieldNote: Fatima is at ease when the world stays the same, and her only goals are small, private ones about getting better at the line. She trusts the union rep to handle any new monitoring, so she doesn't feel she has to act herself. Her pride in quietly improving came out more strongly than any worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company has to share it out fairly, and that's what I'd tell anyone who'd listen. If they're saving money, the workers should get shorter hours or a pay rise, not the sack. I'd sign whatever petition Shona puts round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm the newest on the line and the slowest, so if they cut two people, I know it's me. Last in, first out, that's how our deal works. That frightens me more than I'd say out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd put a bit more aside every month, maybe fifty a week, and stop the takeaways on Friday. I'd go to every union meeting and push for a deal that protects the newer staff, not just the old hands. I'd look at the other plants on the industrial estate too, the crisp factory and the frozen food place, just to know who's hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in my chest, really. Like when you get a brown envelope and you don't want to open it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your line do you think goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The checking, I think. They already have a camera on the filler that rejects underfilled bottles. If it starts reading the caps as well, then what's my half-hourly sheet for? That's the part I'm still slow at anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you won't touch the computer stuff. If the plant offered a paid course on running the new kit, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it's paid and it's in work hours, I'd go, but I'd be dragging my feet. I'm not good with screens, my son does my phone for me. I'd sit at the back and hope Bernie was going too, and I'd hate every minute of it.

S1.say: If the company saves money with machines, the workers should get a share through shorter hours or better pay, not redundancy. She'd sign the union petition and say it to anyone who asked.
S1.think: She's the newest and slowest on the line, so under last in, first out she expects to go first. That scares her more than she lets on.
S1.do: Puts about fifty a week aside and drops the Friday takeaway. Goes to every union meeting to push for protection for newer staff, and quietly checks which plants on the estate are hiring.
S1.feel: A tight chest and dread, like an unopened brown envelope. She still feels she has some say through the union.
S1.quote: I'm the newest on the line and the slowest, so if they cut two people, I know it's me.
S1.fieldNote: Her public line is about fairness and sharing the gains, while her private view is about the seniority rule that puts her at the front of the queue. She'd take a paid course only reluctantly and depends on her son for anything digital. The union is both her shield and the thing she fears won't cover the newest worker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a disgrace and someone in government should have stopped it. I'd be at whatever march there was, and I'd say it online too, which I never do. People like us built these companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I don't think there'd be anything for me. If a robot can fill and cap and fix itself, what's a 43-year-old dinner lady going to do? Imran drives a bus, so if that goes too we're both gone at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop every bit of spending that isn't food, the mortgage or the gas. I'd ring the bank about a payment holiday before we fell behind, and I'd go to the union and the council to find out what help there'd be. I'd ask my brother in Leicester if we could lean on him for a while, though it would kill me to ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, really. Like the floor's gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years' warning, what would you do in the first month after you heard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month, I'd sit down at the kitchen table with Imran and the bank statements, which we never do, and work out how many weeks we'd last. Three months, maybe four if we ate beans. Then I'd go to Shona and say what's the plan, because the union would have to do something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Zara and Adam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them Mum and Dad will sort it, which would be a lie. Zara's fourteen, she'd see through it, she'd hear us at night. Adam's ten, he'd just want to know if he still gets his football boots.

S2.say: It's a disgrace and government should have stopped it. She'd join a march and even post online, which she never does, because people like her built these companies.
S2.think: She doesn't see anything left for her if robots can fill, cap and repair the line. Her husband drives a bus, so the family could lose both incomes at once.
S2.do: Cuts all spending except food, mortgage and heating, and asks the bank about a payment holiday before falling behind. Turns to the union and the council for help and, reluctantly, to her brother.
S2.feel: Sick, like the floor has gone. She sees no path she can steer.
S2.quote: If a robot can fill and cap and fix itself, what's a 43-year-old dinner lady going to do?
S2.fieldNote: With two years there's no plan, only triage: counting weeks of savings and asking for help. She still calls herself a dinner lady, which says a lot about how new the factory identity is. The thought of both her and her husband losing work at once is what tips her into panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, really, it shouldn't be allowed to happen to working people without a plan. But with five years I'd say it louder and earlier, before it lands. I'd want our MP to say where the jobs are meant to come from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the same end, just slower. I'd be 48 when it arrives, still with a mortgage, and nobody hires a 48-year-old to do nothing. Maybe Zara's through school by then, which is something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder from day one, maybe a hundred a month on top of what we do now, and try to pay a chunk off the mortgage. I'd push the union to get the company to promise retraining money in writing. I'd go to the MP's surgery on a Saturday, which I've never done in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, all the time, in the background. But not like the floor's gone, more like a leak you can hear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years instead of two. What does the extra time buy you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of breathing room, and time for the union to fight. With two years they'd have nothing. With five, Shona could at least make the company sign something, like a guaranteed payout or a year's notice. And Zara could finish her exams without us falling apart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you'd hate a course. Would you do one if it meant keeping the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it was that or lose the house, I'd do it. I'd be rubbish at first, I'd need someone sat with me, but I'd do it. I just don't want to be told it's my fault for not keeping up.

S3.say: Working people shouldn't have this done to them without a plan. With five years she'd say it louder and earlier, and she'd want her MP to say where the jobs are meant to come from.
S3.think: It's the same ending, only slower, and she'd be 48 with a mortgage when it arrives. The one comfort is that her daughter might be through school by then.
S3.do: Saves about a hundred a month extra and tries to pay down part of the mortgage. Pushes the union to get retraining money and notice terms in writing, and goes to her MP's Saturday surgery for the first time.
S3.feel: A constant background worry, like a leak she can hear. Less sick than the two-year picture, but no lighter.
S3.quote: I just don't want to be told it's my fault for not keeping up.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time mostly buys the union time to bargain and her daughter time to finish school, not a new plan for Fatima herself. She shifted from refusing a course to accepting one if the house was at stake, while bristling at being blamed. Her resistance looks more like fear of failing than stubbornness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got ten years to make sure it's done properly, so let's not waste them. I'd want a law that companies pay into a fund for every worker a robot replaces. I'd say that at the union and I'd vote for whoever promised it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, ten years feels like enough time to get used to it but not enough to start again. I'd be 53. I'd still have years of mortgage left and no pension worth speaking of. I'd probably keep my head down and hope the deal gets done before I need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, not much changes, and that's the honest answer. I'd keep working, keep saving, get on the union's committee for the change, and vote for whoever talks about protecting workers. I'd wait to see what the company actually does before I spent money on anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more steady. Like a hospital appointment that's months away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. What would you do in the next twelve months, when it's still a long way off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next twelve months, I'd go to every meeting and probably end up on the committee, because nobody else wants to. I'd start a savings pot just for when it comes, separate from the emergency money. And I'd ask Gary to show me more on the line, because the better I am, the later I go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you think you'd be working in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I really don't know, and that's the truth. Maybe on the line still, babysitting the robots, if the union gets that deal. Or back in a kitchen somewhere, if people still want a hot dinner cooked by a person.

S4.say: There are ten years to make sure it's done properly. She'd want a law making companies pay into a fund for every worker a robot replaces, and she'd vote for whoever promised it.
S4.think: Ten years is enough to get used to the idea but not enough to start again at 53 with a mortgage and little pension. She'd keep her head down and hope a deal lands in time.
S4.do: Keeps working and starts a separate savings pot for the change. Joins the union's committee, votes for worker protection, asks the line lead to teach her more, and waits to see what the company does before spending anything.
S4.feel: Uneasy but steadier, like a hospital appointment months away. The worry is real but she feels she can act on it.
S4.quote: Ten years feels like enough time to get used to it but not enough to start again.
S4.fieldNote: The long warning gives her room to organise rather than panic, and she imagines herself on the union committee. She still doesn't plan to retrain on her own and pins her hopes on collective deals. Her picture of 2036 swings between minding robots and going back to a kitchen.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no question, because there's no time for anyone to do anything, not the union, not the government, not us. What would help is a proper guarantee, like your wages for a year while you find something, and somebody patient to train you who doesn't make you feel thick. And the bus going too, I can't stop thinking about that, so it would have to be for both of us.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who decides. It's never people like me or Bernie, it's someone in an office who's never stood at a filler. I've been the one who gets cut once already, from the school kitchen, and I'm not sure I've got another fresh start in me.

headlineQuote: I've been the one who gets cut once already, from the school kitchen, and I'm not sure I've got another fresh start in me.
portrait: Fatima Patel, 43, runs the capper on an early-shift bottling line after twelve years as a school dinner lady, and is still the newest and slowest on her team. She trusts the union far more than any screen and leans on her son for anything digital. When AI stalls she is simply relieved, but as soon as machines start taking tasks she sees herself first in the queue under last in, first out. In the fast AGI picture she panics, counting weeks of savings with her bus-driver husband, while more warning turns her toward the union committee and her MP rather than a new career.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because there would be no time for the union, the government or her family to prepare, and her husband's bus job could go at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: A guarantee of a year's wages while she finds something new, and patient training that doesn't make her feel stupid, covering both her and her husband.
